title: Which two months are these Jodhpur days from?
description: Eight temperature readings for each of two days in Jodhpur are drawn as a double bar graph with a scale of four degrees a unit. The ranges and means of the two days suggest which seasons they belong to.
teaching_notes: One idea: the scale turns a temperature into a bar height, and the lowest, highest and mean of a day hint at its season. Watch for students who use one reading instead of the whole day.

source: Temperature over two days in Jodhpur: draw a double bar graph with 1 unit = 4 degrees Celsius and guess which two months the days belong to
video_script.why: The child can draw a double bar graph and now uses it to reason about a pattern in the data.
video_script.substitution: Draw a pair of bars for each time, then read the lowest, highest and mean of each day.
video_script.anchor: Times: 12 am, 3 am, 6 am, 9 am, 12 pm, 3 pm, 6 pm, 9 pm. Day 1 in degrees Celsius: 20, 18, 16, 20, 26, 34, 30, 24. Day 2: 37, 34, 30, 33, 37, 43, 42, 39. Scale 1 unit = 4 degrees.
video_script.payoff_line: Day one is likely a winter day and day two a summer day.

final_answer.value: Day 1 is likely a winter day (December or January) and Day 2 a summer day (May or June)
final_answer.spoken: day one is likely a winter day, and day two a summer day

maths_rules: bar heights with 1 unit = 4 degrees: 20 / 4 = 5 units and 43 / 4 = 10.75 units
Day 1: lowest 16, highest 34, range 34 - 16 = 18, total 188, mean 188 / 8 = 23.5
Day 2: lowest 30, highest 43, range 43 - 30 = 13, total 295, mean 295 / 8 = 36.875
check: Day 2 is higher than Day 1 at all eight times
video_script.design: One idea: a day's lowest, highest and mean hint at its season. The two rows of readings sit in the anchor; on the board each reading becomes a bar by the scale, and two days are summarised.

<bookmark mark='m4'/>Its range is thirteen degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, find the mean of each day. Day one adds up to one hundred and eighty eight.

<bookmark mark='m3'/>Day two adds up to two hundred and ninety five.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Its mean is thirty six point eight seven five degrees.
